title: SpeakOut Student Wellbeing Handbook
subtitle: A practical guide to mental health, confidence, resilience, relationships, and personal growth
author: SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach
description: A flagship SpeakOut handbook designed to help students understand wellbeing, manage stress, build confidence, develop healthy relationships, and create a personal wellbeing plan.
content:
Chapter 1: Welcome to SpeakOut

Your Wellbeing Journey Begins

Wellbeing is the overall state of your emotional, mental, social and physical health while you live, learn and grow. It is not a fixed trait you either have or lack — it moves throughout the week depending on sleep, stress, relationships and what is happening in your life. Everyone's wellbeing needs attention sometimes, not just people going through an obvious crisis.

This course introduces the ideas, language and practical skills covered in the SpeakOut Student Wellbeing Handbook. Each module pairs a short lesson with a reflection activity and a short knowledge check, so you can build understanding gradually rather than all at once.

There is no requirement to share anything personal with anyone else to complete this course. The reflection questions are for your own thinking; what matters for completion is that you engage honestly with the material and pass each knowledge check.

If anything in this course brings up something you are struggling with, that is a normal and valid response — not a sign you are doing the course wrong. Module 15 covers how and when to ask for support, and you do not have to wait until then to reach out to a trusted adult, school counsellor or local mental health service if you need to.

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions. There are no right answers — they are here to help you notice where you already are before the course begins.

  1. What does wellbeing mean to you?
  2. Which area of your wellbeing needs the most attention right now?
  3. Who are three trusted people you can talk to?

Reflection

  1. What does wellbeing mean to you?
  2. Which area of your wellbeing needs the most attention right now?
  3. Who are three trusted people you can talk to?

Chapter 2: What Is Mental Health?

Understanding the foundation

Mental health refers to your emotional, psychological and social wellbeing — it shapes how you think, feel, handle stress, relate to others and make decisions. Like physical health, everyone has mental health, and it exists on a spectrum rather than as a simple “healthy” or “unhealthy” label. It can be strong in some seasons of life and more fragile in others.

A common myth is that mental health struggles mean something is “wrong” with a person, or that only certain people experience them. In reality, mental health difficulties are common and can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or how someone appears on the outside. Struggling does not mean weakness, and it is not something a person chooses.

Another myth is that mental health only matters once things become severe. In practice, small, regular habits — sleep, movement, connection with others, and having language to describe how you feel — support mental health long before a crisis point, in the same way brushing your teeth prevents problems rather than only treating them.

This course does not diagnose or treat any condition. It offers general education, language and coping skills. If you are ever concerned about your own mental health or someone else's, speak with a trusted adult, school counsellor or qualified professional.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What mental health myths have you heard?
  2. How can schools make it safer for students to speak up?
  3. What is one fact about mental health you want others to know?

Reflection

  1. What mental health myths have you heard?
  2. How can schools make it safer for students to speak up?
  3. What is one fact about mental health you want others to know?

Chapter 3: Knowing Yourself

Self-awareness and growth

Self-awareness is the ability to notice your own thoughts, feelings, values and patterns of behaviour — and to understand how they affect your choices. It is a skill, not a fixed personality trait, which means it can be practised and strengthened over time.

One useful starting point is identifying your strengths: the things you are naturally good at or that come easily to you. Strengths are not only academic or athletic — they include things like listening well, staying calm under pressure, being organised, or making others feel included.

Values are what matters most to you — honesty, fairness, family, creativity, achievement, and so on. When your daily choices line up with your values, you tend to feel more grounded; when there is a gap between what you value and how you are actually spending your time, that gap is often a source of stress worth noticing.

Self-awareness also includes recognising habits you would like to change. Growth does not require becoming a different person — it means noticing a pattern, understanding what triggers it, and choosing one small, realistic adjustment at a time.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What are three strengths you have?
  2. What value matters most to you?
  3. What is one habit you want to improve?

Reflection

  1. What are three strengths you have?
  2. What value matters most to you?
  3. What is one habit you want to improve?

Chapter 4: Understanding Emotions

Naming, accepting, and managing feelings

Emotions are signals — they give you information about what is happening in your life and what you might need. All emotions, including uncomfortable ones like anger, sadness, jealousy or fear, are normal and serve a purpose. The goal is not to eliminate difficult emotions but to recognise, name and respond to them in healthy ways.

Naming an emotion accurately — for example, noticing that what feels like anger is actually hurt, or that anxiety is layered under excitement — tends to make it easier to manage. This is sometimes called “emotional vocabulary,” and it grows with practice, the same way any vocabulary does.

Accepting an emotion means acknowledging it is present without judging yourself for feeling it. This is different from acting on every emotional impulse. You can feel intense anger and still choose how you respond — the feeling and the action are two separate steps.

Healthy ways to manage strong emotions include pausing before reacting, physical movement, talking to someone you trust, writing your thoughts down, and slow breathing. What works varies from person to person, so it is worth trying a few approaches to find what genuinely helps you.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. Which emotion do you find hardest to express?
  2. What helps you calm down safely?
  3. How can you express anger without hurting yourself or others?

Reflection

  1. Which emotion do you find hardest to express?
  2. What helps you calm down safely?
  3. How can you express anger without hurting yourself or others?

Chapter 5: Managing Stress

Pressure, coping, and balance

Stress is your body and mind's response to pressure or demand — exams, deadlines, family responsibilities, or social situations. In small amounts, stress can be motivating and help you focus. Problems tend to arise when stress is constant, feels unmanageable, or has no outlet.

A useful first step in managing stress is identifying your specific triggers. Stress is easier to respond to once you can name what is actually causing it, rather than experiencing it as one large, vague weight.

Healthy coping strategies include breaking large tasks into smaller steps, planning your time realistically, physical activity, sufficient sleep, and talking to someone about what is on your mind. Coping strategies that provide short-term relief but add long-term harm — such as avoiding responsibilities entirely, or using substances to numb stress — tend to make the underlying pressure worse over time.

It is also worth noticing when a responsibility feels too big to face. Breaking it into smaller, concrete steps — the next single action rather than the whole task — usually makes it feel more manageable and reduces the urge to avoid it altogether.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What are your top three stress triggers?
  2. What is one healthy coping skill you can practice this week?
  3. What responsibility can you break into smaller steps?

Reflection

  1. What are your top three stress triggers?
  2. What is one healthy coping skill you can practice this week?
  3. What responsibility can you break into smaller steps?

Chapter 6: Anxiety and Worry

Calming the mind

Anxiety is your body's alarm system — it prepares you to respond to a perceived threat, even when the “threat” is a test, a social situation, or an uncertain future rather than immediate physical danger. Occasional worry is a normal part of life. It becomes more difficult to manage when it is frequent, intense, or interferes with daily activities like sleeping, eating or attending school.

Anxiety often shows up physically — a racing heart, tight chest, upset stomach, or restlessness — before it is fully recognised as a thought. Learning to notice these body signals early can help you respond before worry escalates.

Grounding techniques help bring attention back to the present moment when worry feels overwhelming. Common examples include slow, deliberate breathing; naming five things you can see, four you can hear and three you can touch; or focusing on a single physical sensation, like your feet on the floor.

Occasional worry is manageable with these everyday tools. If anxiety is frequent, intense, or is stopping you from doing things you need or want to do, that is a signal worth taking seriously — it is appropriate and encouraged to speak with a trusted adult, school counsellor or qualified mental health professional.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What does worry feel like in your body?
  2. Which grounding technique can you try?
  3. When should someone seek extra support for anxiety?

Reflection

  1. What does worry feel like in your body?
  2. Which grounding technique can you try?
  3. When should someone seek extra support for anxiety?

Chapter 7: Building Resilience

Recovering from setbacks

Resilience is the ability to recover, adapt and keep functioning after a setback, disappointment or difficult experience. It is often misunderstood as never struggling — in reality, resilience is about how you respond and recover after struggle, not about avoiding hardship altogether.

Resilience is built, not simply inherited. Factors that strengthen it include having supportive relationships, developing problem-solving skills, practising self-compassion instead of harsh self-criticism, and maintaining a sense that your actions can make a difference in your own life.

Reframing a setback — asking “what can I learn from this?” instead of only “why did this happen to me?” — does not erase the disappointment, but it can shift a setback from feeling purely like failure to feeling like useful information for next time.

Recovering from a setback also does not mean pretending it did not hurt. Acknowledging the disappointment honestly, giving yourself time, and then identifying one next step is usually more sustainable than forcing immediate positivity.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. Describe a setback you survived.
  2. What helped you recover?
  3. What lesson did you learn from that experience?

Reflection

  1. Describe a setback you survived.
  2. What helped you recover?
  3. What lesson did you learn from that experience?

Chapter 8: Healthy Relationships

Respect, boundaries, and communication

Healthy relationships — friendships, family relationships, and romantic relationships — share common features: mutual respect, honesty, trust, and the ability to disagree without the relationship being threatened. No relationship is conflict-free; what distinguishes a healthy one is how conflict is handled.

A boundary is a limit you set about what you are and are not comfortable with — how you want to be spoken to, how much time you can give, or what topics you are willing to discuss. Setting a boundary is not the same as rejecting a person; it is a normal, healthy part of any relationship, and people who respect you will generally respect your boundaries too.

Respectful communication includes listening without interrupting, using “I feel” statements instead of blame, and checking that you have understood the other person before responding. These skills reduce the chance that a disagreement escalates unnecessarily.

Warning signs of an unhealthy relationship include consistent disrespect, control over who you see or what you do, pressure to do things you are uncomfortable with, and refusal to accept a boundary once it has been clearly stated. If you notice these patterns in your own relationships, it is worth talking to a trusted adult.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What does respect look like in friendship?
  2. What boundary do you need to set?
  3. How can you handle conflict more calmly?

Reflection

  1. What does respect look like in friendship?
  2. What boundary do you need to set?
  3. How can you handle conflict more calmly?

Chapter 9: Self-Esteem and Confidence

Seeing yourself with value

Self-esteem is the overall sense of your own worth, while confidence often refers more specifically to belief in your ability to handle a particular task or situation. Both can fluctuate — it is normal to feel confident in one area of life and unsure in another.

A common obstacle to healthy self-esteem is the “inner critic” — an automatic negative thought pattern that exaggerates flaws or mistakes. Learning to notice these thoughts and question whether they are actually accurate, rather than accepting them automatically, is a core self-esteem skill.

Confidence tends to build through action rather than waiting to feel ready first. Small, achievable steps — trying something new, speaking up once, completing a task you were avoiding — create real evidence of capability that gradually builds belief in yourself.

Comparing yourself to others, especially on social media where people typically only share their highlights, tends to distort self-esteem. It is more useful to compare your progress to your own past, rather than to someone else's curated presentation of their life.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What negative thought do you need to challenge?
  2. What is one thing you are proud of?
  3. What action can build your confidence this week?

Reflection

  1. What negative thought do you need to challenge?
  2. What is one thing you are proud of?
  3. What action can build your confidence this week?

Chapter 10: Digital Wellbeing

Social media, safety, and balance

Digital wellbeing is about how technology and social media affect your mood, sleep, relationships and sense of self — and making intentional choices about your use, rather than using devices purely on autopilot.

Social media often shows a curated highlight reel rather than everyday reality. Comparing your ordinary day to someone else's best moments is an unfair comparison that can quietly affect mood and self-esteem over time, even when you know intellectually that it is not a complete picture.

Practical digital wellbeing habits include noticing how you feel during and after scrolling, setting boundaries around screen use before bed (screen light and stimulating content can interfere with sleep), being selective about who and what you follow, and taking deliberate breaks from platforms that consistently leave you feeling worse.

Online safety also matters: protecting personal information, being cautious about who you share images or details with, and recognising and reporting cyberbullying — whether it happens to you or someone you know — rather than assuming it must be dealt with alone.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How does social media affect your mood?
  2. What digital habit do you want to change?
  3. How can you protect yourself online?

Reflection

  1. How does social media affect your mood?
  2. What digital habit do you want to change?
  3. How can you protect yourself online?

Chapter 11: Study Skills and Balance

Learning without burnout

Effective studying is less about the number of hours spent and more about how that time is used. Techniques like spacing study sessions out over several days (rather than cramming), testing yourself on material instead of just re-reading it, and studying in short focused blocks with real breaks tend to produce better results with less exhaustion.

Burnout is a state of physical and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged pressure without adequate recovery. Early signs include persistent tiredness even after resting, declining motivation, irritability, and finding it harder to concentrate than usual. Recognising these signs early makes them easier to address before they become severe.

Balance does not mean never working hard — it means making sure rest, sleep, movement and connection with others have a genuine place alongside your responsibilities, rather than being treated as optional extras only allowed once everything else is finished.

Realistic weekly planning — writing down what actually needs to happen and roughly when, rather than keeping it all in your head — tends to reduce the background anxiety of feeling like you might be forgetting something important.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What study habit works best for you?
  2. What is one sign you may need rest?
  3. How can you plan your week better?

Reflection

  1. What study habit works best for you?
  2. What is one sign you may need rest?
  3. How can you plan your week better?

Chapter 12: Physical Health and Mental Health

The body-mind connection

Physical health and mental health are closely connected — what affects the body tends to affect mood, concentration and emotional regulation, and vice versa. This is sometimes called the body-mind connection, and it is one of the most well-established general ideas in wellbeing education.

Sleep is one of the most influential factors. Insufficient or irregular sleep is linked to lower mood, reduced concentration and greater difficulty managing stress. A consistent sleep routine — similar bedtime and wake time most days — tends to support both physical and mental wellbeing more than occasional long “catch-up” sleep.

Regular movement, even in modest amounts like walking, tends to support mood and stress management, partly through its physical effects and partly by providing a break from other pressures. It does not need to mean intense exercise to be beneficial.

Nutrition and hydration also play a role — skipping meals or being significantly dehydrated can affect concentration, energy and irritability. None of these habits are a cure for a mental health condition on their own, but they are a meaningful, practical foundation that supports overall wellbeing.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How many hours do you sleep on most nights?
  2. What physical habit affects your mood?
  3. What small health habit can you improve?

Reflection

  1. How many hours do you sleep on most nights?
  2. What physical habit affects your mood?
  3. What small health habit can you improve?

Chapter 13: Purpose and Goals

Direction, motivation, and meaning

A sense of purpose — having something that feels meaningful to work toward — is associated with greater motivation and resilience during difficult periods. Purpose does not need to be a single grand life mission; it can be as immediate as a value you want to live by this year, or a skill you want to develop.

Goals turn a general sense of direction into something actionable. Clear goals tend to specify what exactly you are working toward, and over what timeframe, rather than staying vague (“I want to do better” versus “I want to improve my grade in this subject by the end of term”).

Large goals can feel overwhelming or distant, which is why breaking them into smaller milestones — and identifying the very next concrete step — makes consistent progress far more achievable than waiting for motivation to arrive fully formed.

It is also normal for goals and sense of purpose to shift over time as you learn more about yourself. Revisiting and adjusting your goals periodically is a sign of healthy self-awareness, not a sign of failure or inconsistency.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What kind of person do you want to become?
  2. What goal matters to you this term?
  3. What is the first small step?

Reflection

  1. What kind of person do you want to become?
  2. What goal matters to you this term?
  3. What is the first small step?

Chapter 14: Helping a Friend

Support without carrying everything alone

Being a supportive friend does not require having all the answers. Often, the most valuable thing you can offer is genuine listening — giving someone your full attention, not interrupting to fix or minimise what they are sharing, and letting them know you believe them and are glad they told you.

Supporting a friend is different from carrying their problem for them. You can care deeply about someone without taking full responsibility for solving what they are going through — especially situations that need adult or professional support, such as abuse, self-harm, or thoughts of suicide.

Some problems should never be kept secret, even if a friend asks you to promise not to tell anyone. If a friend's safety is at risk — for example, they mention self-harm, suicide, abuse, or another situation where someone could be seriously hurt — the caring and responsible response is to tell a trusted adult, even though it may feel like breaking their trust in the moment. A safe friend is not always a silent one.

If you are supporting a friend through something difficult, it is also important to look after your own wellbeing and talk to a trusted adult yourself — you do not have to carry it entirely alone either.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. How can you listen better?
  2. What problem should never be kept secret?
  3. Who can help if a friend is unsafe?

Reflection

  1. How can you listen better?
  2. What problem should never be kept secret?
  3. Who can help if a friend is unsafe?

Chapter 15: Asking for Help

Strength, safety, and support

Asking for help is a sign of self-awareness and strength, not weakness — it means recognising a limit and taking a responsible step to address it, which is exactly what people with strong problem-solving skills do. The idea that people should always manage alone is a myth that stops many people from getting support earlier, when it is often easier to help.

Signs that someone may need extra support include noticeable changes in mood, sleep, appetite, or behaviour that last more than a couple of weeks; withdrawing from friends and activities they used to enjoy; a persistent sense of hopelessness; or, seriously, talking about wanting to harm themselves or not wanting to be here anymore. These signs apply both to noticing them in yourself and in others.

Common reasons students hesitate to ask for help include fear of being judged, not wanting to be a burden, not knowing who to ask, or believing the problem is not “serious enough.” None of these are good reasons to stay silent — support is available for a wide range of concerns, not only severe ones.

Trusted people to reach out to include a parent or guardian, a teacher or school counsellor, another trusted adult in your life, or a qualified mental health professional. If you or someone you know is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services right away.

Reflect honestly on these questions in your own words.

  1. What signs show someone may need help?
  2. Who are your trusted support people?
  3. What stops students from asking for help?

Reflection

  1. What signs show someone may need help?
  2. Who are your trusted support people?
  3. What stops students from asking for help?

Chapter 16: Your Personal Wellbeing Plan

Turning learning into action

A personal wellbeing plan turns everything covered in this course into something practical you can actually use — rather than information you read once and forget. It does not need to be complicated; a short, honest plan you will actually follow is more useful than an elaborate one you abandon after a week.

A useful wellbeing plan usually includes: your early warning signs (the first signals that your stress or mood is slipping, from earlier modules), a short list of coping tools that genuinely work for you, the names of two or three trusted people you can reach out to, and one or two small daily or weekly habits you want to keep consistent — such as sleep routine, movement, or check-ins with a friend.

Reviewing your plan occasionally — monthly, or after a stressful period — and adjusting it as you learn more about what works for you keeps it useful rather than letting it become outdated.

Completing this course is a starting point, not a finish line. Wellbeing is an ongoing practice, and it is normal to keep learning, adjusting, and reaching out for support as your circumstances change.

Reflect honestly on these questions, and consider writing your answers down somewhere you can return to.

  1. What are your early warning signs?
  2. What coping tools work for you?
  3. What commitments will you make for the next 30 days?

Reflection

  1. What are your early warning signs?
  2. What coping tools work for you?
  3. What commitments will you make for the next 30 days?
